notes.meaning: Before Ruth goes out, the writer introduces Boaz. He was a relative of Naomi's dead husband, Elimelech. The words for "prominent man" can mean strength, wealth, and good character all together. Matthew Henry notes that this rich man had poor relatives, and that Naomi did not boast about him or lean on him when she came home in need.

To glean means to pick up the grain the harvesters left behind. God's law let the poor, widows, and foreigners do this. Still, Ruth knew a farmer might refuse her, so she humbly hoped to find someone kind. She shows humility, a willingness to work hard, and respect for Naomi by asking her first.

Ruth just "happened" to come to Boaz's part of the field. To her it looked like chance, but God was quietly guiding her steps. Fields then had no fences, only boundary stones, so she had no idea whose land it was. Matthew Henry says God often works great things through small events that seem like luck to us.

Boaz greets his workers with a blessing, and they bless him back. This shows real faith in everyday work and a warm bond between a good master and his workers. Their words admit that every good thing comes from God's presence and blessing.

Boaz notices a stranger and asks his foreman about her. The foreman was the man in charge of the field workers. Boaz asks "whose" she is, meaning which family she belongs to, since in that culture a young woman was usually known by her family.

The foreman knows Ruth's story. She is the woman from Moab who came back with Naomi. Matthew Henry notes that this report was a good one. She was a poor foreigner, she was linked to Boaz's own family, and she had come to live among God's people.

Ruth did not push in. She politely asked permission to glean. Then she worked steadily from early morning, taking only a short rest in the shelter set up in the field. Her modesty and hard work are what the foreman wants Boaz to know.

Boaz speaks to Ruth kindly, like a father, which suggests he was older. He tells her to stay in his fields near his women workers, where she would be safe and proper company. He orders the young men not to harm her, and he lets her drink from the workers' water jars. He gives her both protection and refreshment.

Ruth bows to the ground, the deepest sign of respect. She is amazed that he would notice her, a foreigner. She came from Moab, a people who had been enemies of Israel. She humbly sees his kindness as a gift she did not deserve.

Boaz has heard all about Ruth's loyalty to Naomi. She left her parents and homeland to live among a people she did not know, much as Abraham once did. Matthew Henry says Boaz especially honors her for leaving everything to follow the true God.

Boaz prays that God will reward Ruth fully. The picture of God's "wings" means his care and protection, like a mother bird sheltering her chicks. Ruth had come to trust in Israel's God. Gill notes that this reward comes from God's grace (his free kindness), not as wages Ruth has earned.

Ruth humbly thanks Boaz and hopes he will keep showing her favor. His kind words have comforted her heart. She says she is not even equal to one of his servant girls. She shows real humility and gratitude.

At lunch Boaz invites Ruth to eat with his workers. She dips her bread in a sour, refreshing sauce, and Boaz himself hands her roasted grain. She eats until she is full and saves the rest for Naomi. Matthew Henry notes that she ate only what she needed so she could keep working.

Boaz lets Ruth glean even among the bundles, which gleaners were not normally allowed to do. He tells his men to pull out stalks on purpose and leave them for her, and not to shame or scold her. This went far beyond what the law required. Matthew Henry (Concise) sees in Boaz's kindness a picture of the kindness of Jesus to poor sinners.

Ruth worked until evening. Then she beat the grain out of the stalks with a stick so it was easy to carry. She had about an ephah of barley, roughly a bushel, which was a very good day's work. Matthew Henry says many small handfuls add up, and honest work brings its reward.

Ruth carried the grain home herself and showed Naomi. She also gave Naomi the food she had saved from lunch. Matthew Henry notes that after working hard in the field, she showed love and care at home.

Naomi sees how much Ruth brought home and asks where she worked. She blesses whoever helped her, even before she knows who it was. Matthew Henry and Wesley suggest a good question to ask ourselves each night: "Where have I gleaned today?" What have I learned, and how have I grown in God's grace?

Hearing the name Boaz, Naomi blesses him. She sees kindness shown to the living (herself and Ruth) and to the dead (her husband and sons). She tells Ruth that Boaz is a "kinsman-redeemer": a close relative who had the right to buy back family land and help a struggling family. Matthew Henry sees Jesus as our true Redeemer, the one who has the right to rescue us.

differ.view: Some read the kindness as the LORD's, not Boaz's. God has not stopped being kind to the family, even after the men died, because he is caring for their widows.

notes.meaning: Ruth adds that Boaz told her to stay with his workers until the whole harvest was done, both barley and wheat. Here "young men" means all his workers, men and women. Matthew Henry and Wesley note that Ruth tells of Boaz's kindness but does not repeat the praise he gave her.

Naomi agrees that staying with Boaz's women workers is wise. In another field Ruth might be mistreated. Going elsewhere might also look like she was scorning Boaz's kindness. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown suggest Naomi was already sensing that Boaz cared for Ruth.

Ruth followed Naomi's advice. She gleaned in Boaz's fields through both the barley and wheat harvests and came home to Naomi each night. Keil & Delitzsch see a quiet hint that things will change once the harvest ends. Matthew Henry says her humility and hard work would lead to honor.
